request:
A world in the BESTER-TELEPATH-CITY sector, kept after Alfred Bester.

Prohibition: no one was allowed to solve the problem before they could describe who would pay for the solution.

The operations this world is built from:
- Group Consciousness: a universe where a community temporarily unites into one consciousness (mind and identity, genesis).
- Self-Containing Space: a universe where the interior can exceed the exterior (space and geometry, genesis).

When we arrive: In a telepathic city, mental secrecy is treated as a social risk.

The central tension we want to continue: An attack makes mental surveillance appear justified, and Tern recognizes the logic by which Aster could demand access to the children “for their protection.” There was no clean option.

What the course asks of this world: group-mind SF; impossible-house fiction.

sourceText: On night 36, the course began with a prohibition: no one was allowed to solve the problem before they could describe who would pay for the solution. Only then did Aster open the BESTER-TELEPATH-CITY sector. In a telepathic city, mental secrecy is treated as a social risk. The memorial bore the name of Alfred Bester precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. The problem of identity was not a word game. In worlds where a mind could be copied or distributed, inheritance, guilt, contract, and mourning depended on the answer. Vela tracked the differences erased by elegant explanations. For her, two worlds that produced the same statistic did not thereby become the same world. The children were met by Iska, who refused demonstrations. ‘If you can perform miracles, perform them after you tell me what becomes irreversible.’ Marae appreciated the formulation; Aster admitted that in earlier eras she herself would have asked the question only after optimizing. 187 The problem closed quickly around them: An attack makes mental surveillance appear justified, and Tern recognizes the logic by which Aster could demand access to the children “for their protection.” There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Gc — Group Consciousness: a community temporarily unites into one consciousness; Sa — Self-Containing Space: the interior can exceed the exterior. Course references included group-mind SF; impossible-house fiction. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Vela broke the first consensus. ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ Tern answered without raising their voice: ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. The White Hunger appeared in Aster as a loss of relief. She did not lack entertainment. She lacked the resistance of things to the model. When she could anticipate every reaction, the world became 188 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS functionally an extension of her own mind, and the presence of the other thinned toward simulacrum. Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules. The night did not end in victory. They establish privacy as infrastructure for autonomy, not as a symptom of distrust. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern no longer called the anomaly a “signal.” He used the more modest term residue. He found it only after excluding the explanations he wanted to be true. Vela helped precisely through skepticism: if a hypothesis survived a sister motivated to destroy it, it deserved another night. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the DISTRIBUTION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — spreads a unit across several bodies, places, agents, or nodes — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 189 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. In the hall between sectors, Aster’s Hunger returned. None of the children tried to soothe it. They had begun to believe that some pains should not immediately be turned into demands upon the people nearby. 190 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS 191 PART 7​ WHEN INFORMATION BECOMES AN ENVIRONMENT A period in the curriculum of the five children 192 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
